name: Lingala, langue du Haut-Congo / 'congolais'
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 6 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: De Boeck, Egide. 1904. Grammaire et vocabulaire du lingala ou langue du Haut-Congo. Bruxelles: Polleunis & Ceuterick, imprimeurs. 176 pp. (archive.org grammaireetvoca00boecgoog, Google Books scan, not in copyright)
catalog_locator: Chapitre I, § 6 'Accent', pp. 11-12 (pp. 17-18 of archive.org grammaireetvoca00boecgoog)
catalog_quote: 6. Accent. — 1. L'accent tombe sur la première syllabe du radical; si celui-ci est monosyllabique, sur le préfixe. Ex.: mòtu: homme. lìsu: œil. molàngi: bouteille. bìla: arracher. bwàka: jeter, rejeter. tàndola: étaler (une étoffe). mokèngeli: gardien. pàlangana; s'éparpiller. ebàndemeli: ce qui attache, mortier, ciment. Cette règle n'est pas absolue; ainsi l'on dit: liwalatàta: espèce de lézard. litungùlu: oignon. mosumàne: scie. angìnya: rassembler. [p. 12] De même quelques radicaux monosyllabiques ont l'accent, surtout s'ils sont formés d'une diphtongue: Ex.: monò: remède, médecine. mowà: épidémie. bobè: mal. mosài: doigt. mondjòi: abeille. Note. — 1. Il arrive que l'accent tonique se déplace par l'addition ou le changement d'un suffixe. En outre, beaucoup de mots ont des accents toniques secondaires, outre leur accent principal. Ex.: bùngutàna: rouler (neutre). bùngutinya: rouler (actif), faire rouler. 2. La syllabe qui porte l'accent n'est pas nécessairement une syllabe longue. Il est difficile de donner des règles fixes à ce sujet. La question de l'accent a une grande importance en congolais, comme en toute langue d'ailleurs. Le mettre à sa place est une des conditions essentielles pour se faire comprendre.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: 6. Accent. 1. The accent falls on the first syllable of the radical (stem); if the stem is monosyllabic, on the prefix. E.g. mòtu 'man', lìsu 'eye', molàngi 'bottle', bìla 'pull out', bwàka 'throw', tàndola 'spread out (cloth)', mokèngeli 'guardian'. This rule is not absolute; thus one says liwalatàta 'kind of lizard', litungùlu 'onion', mosumàne 'saw'. [p.12] Note 1. The tonic accent may move when a suffix is added or changed. Moreover, many words have secondary tonic accents besides their main accent. 2. The accented syllable is not necessarily a long syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main accent on the stem-initial syllable (the noun/verb radical's first syllable); when the radical is a single syllable the accent retracts to the class prefix; some lexical exceptions carry accent later in the word; suffixation can shift it.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Beaucoup de mots ont des accents toniques secondaires, outre leur accent principal' (example bùngutàna / bùngutìnya); position not stated. (Stapleton 1914 for the related river lingua franca: secondary accent on the penult in words of more than three syllables.)
new_statements.exceptions: Rule 'n'est pas absolue': liwalatàta, litungùlu, mosumàne, angìnya accented off the stem-initial syllable; some monosyllabic radicals keep the accent themselves (monò, bobè, mosài, mondjòi), especially diphthongal ones; accent may shift under suffixation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (isolated citation forms of nouns and verbs); author adds that placing the accent correctly is essential to being understood. Pre-tonological 1904 missionary description: the 'accent' very likely conflates lexical high tone; modern descriptions analyse Lingala as a two-tone language and give no word-stress rule for this variety.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.x nort3345 is the Lingala variety 'emanating from the missionary activities in Nouvelle-Anvers and Lisala' (Glottolog comment, citing Meeuwis). The deciding source, De Boeck 1904, is the founding missionary codification of exactly that variety ('lingala ou langue du Haut-Congo', written at Nouvelle-Anvers; Bokamba 2012 ACAL identifies 'Mankanza/Literary Lingala' as the variety codified by E. De Boeck). It is a 1904 pre-tonological, partly prescriptive description; modern sources treat all Lingala as a two-tone language (Meeuwis APiCS survey for Kinshasa Lingala ling1263; Motingea & Bonzoi 2008 'comme en lingala deux tons'). The catalog's existing Lingala unit (ling1263, FSI 1963 penult-stress remark) concerns river/Kinshasa trade Lingala, not this entry. Stapleton 1914 (Bangala lingua franca of the Upper Congo, Bolobo; cf. bang1353) independently gives the same stem-initial rule.

tone_statements.citation: Guthrie, Malcolm. 1940. Tone Ranges in a Two-Tone Language (Lingala). Bulletin of the School of Oriental Studies (University of London) 10(2): 469-478. DOI 10.1017/S0041977X00087632.
tone_statements.quote: Lingala has semantic tones, and many words are distinguished by a difference in tone alone, both nouns and verbs. There is also grammatical intonation ... There are only two levels of tone, High and Mid. Low tone is never used, as every tone is fundamental, and not affected by neighbouring consonants or tones. ... (a) There are only two relative tone levels, normal and high, and almost all tones are static. A semantic falling or rising tone, produced by contraction, is so rare as not to need notice here, and all inflexional tones are static.
tone_statements.locator: p. 470, section 'Intonation' and p. 472, section 'Tone Range' point (a)
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones (high vs mid/'normal'), lexical and grammatical (each verbal inflexion has its tone); noun roots show all 4 patterns, prefixes mostly mid; downdrift near-imperceptible; no stress note.

sources.note: p. xi: Lingala is a tone language (two tones); 'there are many speakers of Lingala who use a stress system instead of tones. Most speakers who use a stress system stress the penultimate syllable'; model speaker uses tone. Variety: trade Lingala 'from Leopoldville upstream' (already the catalog source for ling1263).
